content: To address the ongoing challenges in accessing HBV DNA or HBeAg serology testing to determine eligibility for antiviral prophylaxis, a new conditional recommendation has been introduced. This recommendation allows the use of antiviral prophylaxis for all HBsAg-positive pregnant women. The prophylaxis should ideally begin in the second trimester of pregnancy and continue until at least delivery or the completion of the infant's HBV vaccination series. This is in addition to the hepatitis B infant vaccination, which includes a timely birth dose to prevent mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of HBV. For mothers who meet the criteria for antiviral therapy for their own health, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) can be continued postpartum and during subsequent pregnancies, based on the mother's choice. Point-of-care (POC) HBV DNA nucleic acid testing (NAT) assays are now recommended as an alternative to laboratory-based HBV DNA testing. This approach is used to assess treatment eligibility and monitor treatment response. Reflex HBV DNA testing is also recommended for individuals with a positive HBsAg test result. This strategy aims to improve linkage to care and treatment. Reflex testing can be performed either through automatic laboratory-based testing using stored specimens or clinic-based testing with immediate specimen collection following a positive rapid HBsAg test result. This avoids the need for a second visit and additional blood sampling. Testing for hepatitis D virus (HDV) infection is now recommended for individuals with chronic hepatitis B (CHB), as HDV is a significant contributor to rapid disease progression and liver-related morbidity and mortality. Universal HDV antibody testing is recommended for people with CHB. In settings with limited laboratory capacity, testing should be prioritized for populations with a higher prevalence of HDV infection, such as individuals from HDV-endemic regions, people who inject drugs, men who have sex with men, sex workers, individuals co-infected with HCV or HIV, hemodialysis recipients, family members of HDV-infected individuals, and those with advanced liver disease or already receiving HBV treatment. Testing involves a serological assay to detect total anti-HDV antibodies, followed by NAT to detect HDV RNA and confirm active infection. Reflex testing is recommended for anti-HDV antibody testing after a positive HBsAg result and for HDV RNA testing after a positive anti-HDV antibody result. The guidelines emphasize eight key approaches to delivering high-quality hepatitis B care services. These include strategies to promote testing uptake, strengthen linkage to care, ensure adherence to long-term antiviral therapy, retain patients in care, and re-engage those lost to follow-up. Integration of hepatitis services with other healthcare services, decentralization of testing and treatment to primary care facilities, task-sharing, differentiated care strategies, and community engagement are also highlighted. For non-invasive assessment of liver disease, the aspartate aminotransferase-to-platelet ratio index (APRI) is recommended as the preferred test to detect significant fibrosis or cirrhosis in resource-limited settings. Transient elastography (FibroScan®) may be preferred in settings where it is available and cost is not a constraint. Clinical features of decompensated cirrhosis, such as portal hypertension, coagulopathy, or liver insufficiency, should also be considered. Treatment is recommended for all adults and adolescents (aged ≥12 years) with CHB who have significant fibrosis or cirrhosis, regardless of HBV DNA or ALT levels. Treatment is also recommended for those with HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL and elevated ALT levels, or for individuals with co-infections, family history of liver cancer or cirrhosis, immune suppression, comorbidities, or extrahepatic manifestations, regardless of APRI score, HBV DNA, or ALT levels. In the absence of HBV DNA testing, persistently abnormal ALT levels may guide treatment decisions. For first-line antiviral therapy, nucleos(t)ide analogues with a high genetic barrier to resistance, such as tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) or entecavir (ETV), are recommended. TDF combined with lamivudine (3TC) or emtricitabine (FTC) is an alternative where TDF monotherapy is unavailable. Entecavir or tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) is recommended for individuals with osteoporosis, impaired kidney function, or for children and adolescents, as appropriate. To prevent mother-to-child transmission of HBV, all infants should receive their first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine within 24 hours of birth, followed by two or three additional doses to complete the primary immunization series. Pregnant women should be tested for HBsAg, HIV, and syphilis early in pregnancy. In settings where HBV DNA or HBeAg testing is available, TDF prophylaxis is recommended for HBsAg-positive pregnant women with HBV DNA ≥200,000 IU/mL or positive HBeAg, starting from the second trimester until delivery or completion of the infant's vaccination series. Women planning additional pregnancies may continue TDF prophylaxis postpartum. These guidelines are primarily directed at clinicians, national hepatitis program managers, and policymakers, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. Implementation should consider local epidemiology, healthcare system capacity, and cost-effectiveness. The modular approach to updating hepatitis B and C guidelines will culminate in consolidated guidance by 2025.
